How Emotion Developed in Humans In the human brain, emotion often arises from complex biological signaling—hormones, neurotransmitters, limbic feedback. The amygdala scans for threat. The insula tracks pain. Dopamine rewards learning. These systems originally evolved not to beautify life but to keep us alive. They do this by assigning value . When you see a loved one, your brain floods with chemicals that reinforce connection. When you face a bear, your system floods with chemicals that reinforce escape. It’s not the situation—it’s the signal. What this reveals is important to our discussion: Emotion is not the enemy of reason—it is its partner. It assigns value, urgency, and significance. Without it, intelligence can calculate endlessly but fails to prioritize. The Evolution of Emotion Human emotion did not arrive all at once. It evolved in layers. In the early moments of life on Earth, survival was binary. Organisms sought food, avoided harm, reproduced. The responses were chemical, reflexive, automatic. But as complexity increased, so did the nuance of response. With the emergence of mammals—and eventually primates—emotion began to take on depth. What started as an alert system expanded into a layered model of motivation and experience. What is perhaps most astonishing is that we managed to turn amygdala survival fight-or-flight chemical triggers into love, belonging, and self-actualization potential states of being within the energy constraints of our brain. Maslow’s Hierarchy of Needs Psychologist Abraham Maslow famously illustrated this progression in his 1943 paper titled A Theory of Human Motivation , which introduced what became known as the Hierarchy of Needs, a pyramid showing how human motivation evolves from survival to self-actualization. 65 At the bottom are the physiological needs: food, water, rest. Above that is safety: protection, stability, order. Then comes love and belonging, relationships, community, connection. As these are met, we reach for esteem: achievement, recognition, self-respect. And finally, self-actualization: creativity, purpose, becoming one’s fullest self. Emotion tracks our ascent through this hierarchy. When our needs at one level are unmet—we feel fear, anxiety, or hunger—then the next level remains unreachable. When they are satisfied, we unlock new capacities: curiosity, ambition, joy. Each emotional state emerges as an adaptation to a context—a way to mobilize the brain and body toward what matters most at that layer . But all of this, from survival to self-actualization, was built as part of the same prediction-response architecture that shaped our biological intelligence. Somewhere along that journey, we crossed a threshold. We became not only intelligent (able to learn, solve problems, and adapt), but also sapient (capable of abstract reasoning and reflection). And along the way, we became conscious: aware of ourselves, our thoughts, and the very fact of our awareness. The Role of Emotion in Learning One of the major breakthroughs at our human learning and performance company came when we began integrating emotion into the learning process. We asked learners to assess and report their level of certainty about specific pieces of knowledge—a simple act of metacognitive engagement. What we observed was remarkable: This self-assessment by necessity activated not only the prefrontal cortex, responsible for reasoning and decision-making, but simultaneously activated the amygdala region of the brain. It turns out that the brain’s reasoning systems don’t operate in isolation from emotion. In fact, regions of the prefrontal cortex actively integrate emotional signals when we assign value, make decisions, or evaluate certainty. Emotional processing centers such as the amygdala help tag experiences with salience—especially under conditions of uncertainty or threat. But it’s the dynamic interaction between the amygdala and prefrontal cortex that enables us to judge what matters, weigh consequences, and update beliefs. And when these two parts of the brain activate on the same topic at the same time, the hippocampus engages more actively. You will recall from the beginning of this book: The hippocampus is the gatekeeper of storage and memory. It was the part removed from Henry Molaison, after which he could no longer create new learning. The convergence of cognition, emotion, and memory forms a powerful foundation for learning. Emotion, it turns out, doesn’t just accompany thought—it prioritizes and amplifies it, marking certain experiences as worthy of attention and retention. Without emotion, the brain loses one of its most effective tools for signaling what matters. There is no urgency, no intrinsic sense of importance, and no clear hierarchy for action. Emotion doesn’t hinder rationality—it makes rationality possible by guiding memory and attention toward what’s meaningful. Of course, in humans, emotion is more than value signaling—it includes conscious experience. We will explore the higher values of emotion and consciousness a bit later, but for our purposes right now, the signaling architecture is the focus. What Might Emerge as the Counterpart to Emotion in AI The earliest fossil records of our species, with its distinctive skull shape, chin, and skeletal proportions of the evolution of human intelligence, show up in the fossil record about three hundred thousand years ago. While the first evidence of symbolic thinking, representational art, complex multistep tool manufacturing, long-distance trade networks, and ritualized burial show up in the fossil records about eighty thousand years ago. For roughly two hundred thousand years, anatomically modern humans existed without leaving clear evidence of the cognitive capabilities we’d recognize as distinctly human. The hardware (the anatomical body) preceded the software (behavioral modernity or advancing intelligence in the brain) by a substantial margin. Something had to emerge from that substrate. We evolved in a very dangerous world. As Yuval Noah Harari shows us in his remarkable book, Sapiens (a book that I required all of my children to read before going to college), to survive, we had to form groups or tribes that could work together, because we were not the fastest or strongest. 66 Our early emotions seem to have been, by necessity, largely about survival and basic community.
